p.x:
My grandmother is 82 and my grandfather is 85. They live in a small house near us. My grandmother has grey hair and always wears a big smile. Every morning, she drinks tea and works in the garden. She is very active for her age!
My grandfather walks slowly now because his knee hurts. But he still goes to the market every day. He loves telling stories about when he was young.
They have eight grandchildren, and we all visit them on Sundays. My grandmother cooks a big lunch for everyone. I think my grandparents are the happiest people I know.

In Thailand, families traditionally take care of their older relatives at home. Many grandparents live with their children and help look after the grandchildren. This tradition is still strong, but it is changing.
As people get older, they may need more help. Some need a walking stick or a wheelchair to move around. Others need a hearing aid. Many older people want to stay independent for as long as possible, living in their own homes and doing things for themselves.
When families can't provide enough help, some older people move into a care home, where a professional carer looks after them. In some families, a relative gives up work to care for a parent. This can be very tiring and needs a lot of patience.
It's also important to remember that ageing isn't just about problems. Many older people are healthy, active and full of wisdom. Their wrinkles tell the story of a long life, and they have a lot to teach younger generations. Visiting regularly gives them companionship and helps prevent loneliness. Senior citizens in Thailand also get discounts on public transport, and some study at university after the retirement age as lifelong learners.

Thanks to improvements in healthcare, nutrition and sanitation, life expectancy has risen dramatically over the past century. At the same time, the birth rate in many countries has fallen sharply. The combination has produced an ageing population, and Thailand is ageing faster than almost any other middle-income country.
This demographic shift has profound consequences. As the proportion of older people grows, the workforce shrinks, creating a labour shortage in many industries. Fewer workers must support more retirees, putting pressure on pensions and public finances. Healthcare costs also rise, since older people are more likely to live with a chronic illness or conditions such as dementia, which can cause memory loss and make people increasingly dependent on others.
Families feel the pressure too. Many middle-aged adults belong to the so-called sandwich generation, caring for frail parents while also raising children of their own. Professional nursing is expensive, and the traditional model of large families caring for elderly relatives is becoming harder to sustain.
Yet there are reasons for optimism. Japan, home to tens of thousands of centenarians, shows that longevity can go hand in hand with good health. Researchers point to diet, physical activity and strong social connections as keys to ageing well. Intergenerational programmes, which bring older and younger people together, benefit both groups. Tackling ageism, the assumption that older people have little to contribute, may be one of the most important changes of all.
